items.title: Defaults matter — organ donation rates differ by opt-in vs opt-out
items.claim: Johnson and Goldstein's 2003 paper compared organ donation rates in countries with opt-in (default no) vs opt-out (default yes) systems. What did they find?

options.text: Rates were identical regardless of default
Opt-out countries had effective consent rates of 85-99%; opt-in countries 4-28%. The default radically shaped behaviour even when explicit choice was easy

items.reveal:
Johnson and Goldstein (Science 2003) compared European countries with similar cultures. Germany (opt-in): 12% effective consent; Austria (opt-out): 99.98%. The difference is too large to be preference; it's about the cost of changing the default and what people interpret it as recommending.

The UK moved to opt-out (Wales 2015; England 2020; Scotland 2021) following this evidence. Spain has had high organ donation rates under opt-out plus strong organisational infrastructure for decades.
items.why: Choice architecture has policy effects even when no one's freedom of choice has changed. Defaults are inevitable; designing them deliberately is a choice.

items.title: Comparative advantage is about relative, not absolute, costs
items.claim: Ricardo's 1817 numerical example: Portugal can produce both wine and cloth more efficiently than England (absolute advantage in both). According to comparative advantage, should both countries still trade?

options.text: Yes — both countries benefit from specialising in the good in which they have the lowest opportunity cost. Portugal specialises in wine (relative advantage); England in cloth
Only one country benefits from trade

items.reveal:
Ricardo's 'Principles of Political Economy' (1817) used Portugal-England wine-cloth as a thought experiment, not necessarily descriptive of the actual trade. The insight: even if one country is more productive in everything, gains from trade still arise from differences in relative productivity.

Real-world caveats: factor mobility within countries is imperfect; adjustment costs (displaced workers) can be substantial; gains can be uneven across groups; political economy of trade (David Autor's 'China shock' research on US manufacturing) shows specific losers as well as aggregate gains.
items.why: Comparative advantage is foundational but often taught without the adjustment cost and distributional caveats that determine whether trade liberalisation is politically sustainable.

items.title: Dutch disease named for Netherlands natural gas
items.claim: The 'Dutch disease' concept emerged from observing the Netherlands after its 1959 Groningen natural gas discovery. What's the mechanism?

options.text: Resource exports appreciate the real exchange rate, making non-resource tradable sectors (manufacturing) uncompetitive; when the resource is exhausted or prices fall, the diminished manufacturing base struggles to recover
Resource discovery always raises GDP permanently

items.reveal:
The Economist coined the term in 1977. Corden and Neary (1982) formalised the mechanism in a two-sector model with traded and non-traded goods.

Observed cases: Netherlands itself (1960s-70s); Venezuela's oil dependence; Nigeria; arguably the UK in the North Sea oil era. Counter-examples (Norway's sovereign wealth fund) show institutional design can mitigate the effect.

The broader 'resource curse' literature (Sachs and Warner, Acemoglu and others) extends to institutional and political channels.
items.why: Natural resource booms are mixed blessings. The institutional and macroeconomic management determines whether they fund long-run development or undermine it.
